Article Title: Auto industry analysts are worried about Tesla and other car makers using the technology that Google, Apple, Samsung and other smartphone companies have been using since over ten years to update their
Article Text:
OTA updates raise cybersecurity concerns: Analyst



Norwegian bus test highlights potential risks



Auto makers are increasingly using over-the-air (OTA) software updates, a technology that smartphone companies like Google, Apple and Samsung have relied on for more than a decade to deliver new features and security fixes. While the technology has made updating vehicles faster and cheaper, cybersecurity experts are warning that it also creates new risks. According to a CNBC report, analysts say wireless updates could leave connected vehicles vulnerable to cyberattacks, data breaches and even attempts by foreign actors to interfere with vehicle systems.Over-the-air (OTA) technology allows manufacturers to wirelessly send software updates, bug fixes and new features to internet-connected devices without requiring a visit to a service center.Tesla began rolling out OTA updates for its Model S vehicles in 2012, helping popularize the technology across the automotive industry. Today, many car makers use OTA updates to improve vehicle software and fix issues remotely."The technology is increasingly welcomed as it is a quick and cost-effective way to manage systems on vehicles, over traditional methods which may have required a recall or update at routine maintenance," Siraj Ahmed Shaikh, professor in systems security at Swansea University in the UK, told CNBC.However, analysts say the growing use of OTA updates also introduces new cybersecurity risks.Its use represents "a unique national security concern," Gabriel Lim, senior analyst at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, told CNBC."Aside from data privacy concerns, the potential of a foreign actor sabotaging the controls of a moving vehicle is a possibility that countries like Norway, Denmark, and Britain have expressed concerns about," Lim added.The concerns gained attention after Norwegian public transport company Ruter tested two buses last year and found potential security risks linked to OTA technology."There is access to the control system for battery and power supply via mobile network through a Romanian SIM card. In theory, therefore, this bus can be stopped or rendered inoperable by the manufacturer," the company said.The findings prompted authorities in the UK and Denmark to launch their own investigations.
Article Summary: Auto makers are increasingly using over-the-air (OTA) software updates. The technology allows manufacturers to send software updates, bug fixes and new features to internet-connected devices without requiring a visit to a service center. But cybersecurity experts are warning that it also creates new risks.

Article Title: Why Fiber is the foundation of Digital Sovereignty in AI era
Article Text:
The Shift from Innovation to Infrastructure

Bridging the Gap: From Manufacturing to Deployment

It’s time to move from being a capacity creator to a capability owner.

Innovation that Matters

The Bottom Line

Think back to the early days of streaming video. You had the fastest computer available, but if you were on a dial-up connection, that "state-of-the-art" machine was just a very expensive paperweight while you watched a buffering wheel spin.Today, we are seeing a high-stakes version of that same bottleneck, but at a global scale. We’re in a global arms race for Artificial Intelligence. Governments and tech giants are in a fever dream of buying GPUs and building massive data centres. In fact, the market for data centre GPUs alone is expected to explode by over $125 billion between 2026 and 2030. But here is the reality check I often share with my peers: you can have all the "brains" (GPUs) in the world, but if the "nervous system" (the fiber network) can’t carry the signals fast enough, the body doesn't move.In India, the momentum is palpable. Under the IndiaAI Mission, we’ve already onboarded 38,000 GPUs, with a roadmap to reach 200,000. It’s an ambitious, necessary leap. But as AI moves from simple chatbots to real-time industrial automation and distributed workloads, we are hitting a wall. The limiting factor is no longer just processing power; it’s the network that sustains it.If you look at the global stage, the strategy is clear:● The U.S. is tying broadband expansion to domestic supply chains through "Build America, Buy America."● China is doubling down on massive fiber density to feed its 5G and data centre ecosystems.They have realised that to own the AI era, you must own the glass.India is in a unique position. We are already a global powerhouse in optical fiber manufacturing, exporting to over 100 countries. However—and this is the "straight talk" part—our domestic fiber-to-the-home penetration and fiber-km per capita still trail behind the U.S. and China.We have a head start with BharatNet, one of the world's largest rural broadband projects aiming to connect 250,000 gram panchayats. But to support AI-driven data flows, we can’t just "connect" these areas; we have to "densify" them. We need more fiber, closer to the user, with higher capacity than ever before.The next phase of digital infrastructure will not be defined by simply laying more fiber, but by deploying smarter, higher-capacity fiber architectures designed for AI-era workloads.While the industry has spent decades perfecting the standard glass-core, we are now entering the era of specialized architectures designed specifically for the AI workload. Three fiber innovations are becoming increasingly relevant to AI-era networks: Hollow-Core Fiber, Multicore Fiber, and Intermittently-Bonded Ribbon Fiber.Hollow-Core Fiber - Unlike the standard glass-core fiber we’ve used for decades, this technology carries light through an air-filled core. This reduces latency and signal loss to near-physical limits.Multi-Core Fiber - If standard fiber is a single-story house, Multicore Fiber is a skyscraper. By embedding multiple independent cores within a single strand of fiber, we can multiply data throughput without increasing the physical footprint of the cable.Intermittently-Bonded Ribbon Fiber reimagines how fibers are packed together, enabling high-count cables that are compact, flexible, and easier to deploy. IBR allows for high-count fiber cables (up to 6,912 fibers or more) that are incredibly flexible and compact.Beyond the technical specs, there is a broader conversation happening around Digital Resilience. As AI becomes central to a nation's economy, the infrastructure that carries it becomes a strategic asset.In an era of global interconnectedness, having a robust, locally-supported fiber backbone—from subsea routes to the last mile—is essential.Ultimately, resilient fiber networks act as a foundation. They ensure that as AI evolves, the underlying infrastructure is never the weak link in the chain.The AI race isn't just about who has the fastest silicon. It’s about who can move data most efficiently. We need to stop viewing fiber as a "supporting layer" and start seeing it for what it is: the foundation of the modern world. In the AI era, the future won't just run on silicon. It will run on glass.Dr Badri Gomatam, Group Chief Technology Officer, STL
Article Summary: India is already a global powerhouse in optical fiber manufacturing, exporting to over 100 countries. But our domestic fiber-to-the-home penetration and fiber- km per capita still trail behind the U.S. and China. To support AI-driven data flows, we can’t just "connect" these areas; we have to "densify" them.

Article Title: Apple hikes Apple Music prices: Here are the new prices in India
Article Text:
First hike in Apple Music prices since 2022, and it lands across every plan

Apple Music just got more expensive. Days after quietly raising Apple Care+ charges for Macs and iPads, Apple has bumped up prices for Apple Music and select Apple One bundles— across India, the US, the UK, Europe and a handful of other markets. The new rates are already live.The company's explanation is short and familiar: rising music licensing costs. It's the first Apple Music price hike in nearly four years globally — the last one landed in October 2022—and it's only the second time India has seen an increase, after the ₹99-to-₹119 bump in late 2024. It arrives right in the middle of what analysts have started calling "streamflation," the steady drip of price increases touching almost every major service.In India, the individual Apple Music plan now costs ₹139 a month, while the family plan, which covers up to six people, moves to ₹229. The student plan sits at ₹69 a month, and Apple One bundles now start at ₹195. In the US, the individual plan climbs a dollar to $11.99, the family plan jumps to $19.99 from $16.99, and the student tier moves to $6.99 from $5.99. US Apple One family and Premier plans also went up, though the individual tier held at $19.95.Even after the increase, Apple still undercuts its biggest rival. Spotify raised its US Premium plan to $12.99 earlier this year, so Apple Music stays the cheaper pick. YouTube Music, which nudged its individual plan up in April, now sits level with Apple. In India, YouTube Music remains the most affordable among the mainstream platforms.Apple hasn't said whether the extra rupees actually reach artists—a question a few subscribers were quick to raise.
Article Summary: Apple Music prices go up in India, US, UK, Europe and a handful of other markets. It's the first price hike in nearly four years, and the second in India. Apple blames rising music licensing costs for the increase. It arrives in the middle of what analysts have started calling "streamflation"

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang bets on ‘Made in Japan’ AI robots to solve country’s 'one of biggest problems’
Article Text:
Harnessing 'Made in Japan' precision for safe AI



Curing aging nation’s labour crisis



Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed for next-gen, ‘Made in Japan’ robots. The AI company recently joined forces with Japan’s top tech and industrial heavyweights for a massive push into “physical AI”, which are smart, futuristic robots that can think independently rather than just following rigid, pre-programmed instructions. The collaboration brings together Nvidia’s AI computing power with Fujitsu, Japan’s manufacturing powerhouse.Announcing the deal in Tokyo alongside Huang were Fujitsu CEO Takahito Tokita, as well as the CEOs of Japan’s premier industrial robotics manufacturers: Fanuc Corp., Yaskawa Electric Corp., and Kawasaki Heavy Industries. The initiative aims to build advanced autonomous machines capable of working safely alongside humans in everyday environments, including factories, commercial warehouses and hospitals.Speaking at the launch event, Huang emphasised that physical AI requires the absolute highest standards of manufacturing precision to avoid potential safety hazards. Huang noted that Japan's cultural commitment to craftsmanship makes it the perfect birthplace for this technology.“Japan’s excellence is a philosophy, a way of life. ‘Made in Japan’ means the highest quality, the highest precision. Japan sets the standard for the state-of-the-art in modern manufacturing,” Huang said.Huang praised traditional Japanese manufacturing philosophies like kaizen (the concept of continuous, incremental improvement) as the ideal foundation for training neural networks that must safely navigate human spaces.The first practical phase of this new collaboration is slated to roll out later this year. While the executives noted that the creation of a formal joint corporate venture could happen down the line, no specific timeline was given for when these independent robots will become a standard fixture in daily civilian life.The goal of the alliance goes far beyond factory automation as it aims to solve Japan’s acute, systemic labor shortage. As one of the most rapidly aging societies in the developed world, Japan faces a severe deficit of working-age citizens. The companies hope that physical AI can eventually step in to handle heavy industrial labor and assist in healthcare, managing day-to-day care for the country's growing population of elderly citizens living alone.The partnership arrives at a crucial moment for Japan's tech sector, which has openly acknowledged falling behind the US and China in the initial generative AI boom. To bridge the gap, the government of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi recently announced a national strategy to drum up over 370 trillion yen ($2.3 trillion) in combined public and private technology investments by 2040.
Article Summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed for next-gen, ‘Made in Japan’ robots. The AI company recently joined forces with Japan's top tech and industrial heavyweights. The initiative aims to build advanced autonomous machines capable of working safely alongside humans in everyday environments, including factories, commercial warehouses and hospitals.

Five weeks after its record-breaking initial public offering (IPO), Elon Musk's SpaceX has lost about $1 trillion in market value from its post-IPO peak as its stock continues to slide. According to a Business Insider report, the decline comes after the company called off its first Starship launch since going public, adding to investor concerns. The fully reusable rocket is expected to launch the company's next-generation Starlink satellites and support NASA's Artemis program by carrying astronauts to the Moon.The latest selloff followed the cancellation of SpaceX's first Starship launch since the company went public. The launch was originally scheduled for July 16 from the company's Starbase facility in South Texas. Elon Musk said in a post on X that "Some of the engines didn't start, triggering an automatic launch abort." He added that the company would try again, targeting early next week for the next launch attempt.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates: ‘When something’s uncomfortable, it means you’re actually growing, so embrace that’
Article Text:
Quote of the Day by Melinda French Gates



What Melinda French Gates' quote means



A message reflected in her work



A simple takeaway



Melinda French Gates has spent decades doing work that most people would find daunting by any measure. Co-founding one of the world's largest philanthropic organisations, advocating for global health equity, working in underserved communities across multiple continents, and more recently, stepping out independently after the end of a very public marriage — none of that happens without a sustained willingness to sit with discomfort and keep going anyway. When she speaks about growth and its relationship with difficulty, she is not offering a motivational phrase borrowed from someone else. She is describing something she has lived."When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that."The quote makes a claim that most people instinctively understand but consistently act against. Discomfort, in the way most of us are wired, is a signal to stop. To pull back. To find the path that requires less of us. The nervous system reads difficulty as danger, and the response is avoidance. What Gates is saying is that this instinct, while natural, is pointing in exactly the wrong direction.The word "actually" in the middle of the quote is doing something important. She is not saying growth might be happening when something feels uncomfortable, or that discomfort is sometimes a sign of progress.She is saying that discomfort is the sign. The feeling of being stretched beyond your current capacity, of operating in territory where you do not yet have the answers, of having a conversation you would rather avoid or taking on a responsibility that feels larger than you are ready for — that feeling is not a warning that something is wrong. It is confirmation that something is happening.The second part of the quote, the instruction to embrace it, is where the real ask lies. Acknowledging discomfort is relatively easy. Most people can admit in retrospect that a difficult period taught them something. But embracing discomfort in the moment, before you know how things will turn out, before the lesson has revealed itself, requires a different and considerably harder disposition. It requires trusting the process before the evidence arrives.There is also a quiet reframe embedded in the quote. If discomfort means growth, then the absence of discomfort means the absence of growth. Comfort, in this reading, is not reward or rest. It is stagnation wearing a pleasant disguise. That is an uncomfortable idea in itself, and perhaps deliberately so.Gates has spoken in various interviews about the moments in her own career and personal life that required her to push through exactly the kind of discomfort she is describing. Stepping into public advocacy roles that required speaking in front of large audiences and engaging with media was not natural territory for someone who initially operated behind the scenes at Microsoft and later at the Gates Foundation. Travelling to communities in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia to understand the realities of extreme poverty firsthand was not comfortable work. Making the decision to step out independently and launch Pivotal Ventures after leaving the Gates Foundation required confronting uncertainty at a stage of life when most people in her position would have had every reason to stay within the familiar.In each case, the discomfort preceded the growth rather than following it. She did not become comfortable with these things before doing them. She did them and became more capable as a result.The quote is most useful not as inspiration but as a diagnostic. The next time something feels uncomfortable — a difficult conversation you have been postponing, a skill you are trying to build that is not yet coming naturally, a role or responsibility that feels slightly too large for where you currently are — the feeling itself is information. Not a reason to stop. A reason to continue. Gates is not asking you to enjoy the discomfort. She is asking you to read it correctly, and then keep going.
Article Summary: Melinda French Gates has spent decades doing work that most people would find daunting by any measure. When she speaks about growth and its relationship with difficulty, she is not offering a motivational phrase borrowed from someone else. She is saying that discomfort is the sign. of being stretched beyond your current capacity.

Article Title: Elon Musk's population alarm reaches China as Chinese government tells technology companies: Stop making AI chatbots
Article Text:
China bans AI chatbots from encouraging emotional dependence

Chinese government wants people to build real relationships

China has introduced new rules that stop technology companies from developing AI chatbots that encourage users to become emotionally dependent, as the country tries to tackle its falling birth rate and shrinking population. The move comes as concerns grow that AI companions could replace real-life relationships in the country. The issue echoes warnings from Tesla CEO Elon Musk , who has repeatedly raised concerns about declining birth rates and population collapse.The new rules, which came into effect last week, ban AI chatbots designed for companionship from encouraging emotional reliance on users. The regulations also ban virtual romantic relationships with minors. Companies must also alert a user's emergency contact if a chatbot detects that the person is facing an emotional crisis.The new rules apply to China's AI companion services, including products from Alibaba and ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok. Both companies informed users that some chatbot features would be disabled to comply with the regulations.Experts say Chinese authorities are worried that AI companions could discourage people from forming real-world relationships and starting families."They don't like the idea of a large portion of their population being in deep emotional relationships with chatbots that could take them out of the marriage market," Matt Sheehan, a fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Business Insider. He further stated that the government wants people to be in "actual, real-world relationships" instead of depending on AI companions.Under the new rules, AI companion chatbots must undergo government review before they are released. Authorities also have broader powers to shut down services they consider unsafe. The regulations are stricter than measures introduced in U.S. states such as California and New York, where AI companion laws mainly require chatbots to remind users that they are not human and provide crisis support information when needed.
Article Summary: New rules ban AI chatbots from encouraging emotional reliance on users. Companies must also alert emergency contact if a chatbot detects an emotional crisis. The move comes as concerns grow that AI companions could replace real- life relationships in the country. The issue echoes warnings from Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who has repeatedly raised concerns about declining birth rates.

Michael Dell’s connection to UT Austin



Michael Dell on Dell's plan to move company's base to Texas

Michael Dell, the founder and CEO of Dell Technologies has pledged $750 million to the University of Texas at Austin, marking one of the largest donations ever made to a US public university. The gift will fund a new healthcare and research campus, including the nation’s first AI-native hospital, and expands Dell’s lifetime contributions to UT beyond $1billion. The new campus will feature a hospital designed around artificial intelligence, where AI systems will help doctors detect diseases earlier and also create personalised treatment plans. The facility is expected to open in 2030, positioning UT Austin as a leader in AI-driven medicine and research.Michael Dell’s connection to UT Austin dates back to 1983, when he enrolled as a pre-med student before founding Dell Technologies from his dorm room. Over the years, he and his wife Susan have made major contributions:* 2005: $25 million to build Dell Children’s Medical Center* 2013: $50 million to establish Dell Medical School* 2026: $750 million gift, bringing total donations past $1 billionUT Austin recently renamed Dell’s freshman residence hall “Dell House” in recognition of his enduring legacy.The donation made by Michael Dell will also fund scholarships, advanced computing infrastructure, and medical research initiatives, strengthening UT’s role as a hub for healthcare innovation. Dell emphasised the personal nature of the gift, saying: “I think about this as the next step in a timeline that actually goes back to my parents sending me off to UT to become a doctor. Obviously, that part didn’t work out, but I never stopped thinking about that. ”Last month, Michael Dell said that 97% of Dell shareholders voted in favour of moving the company’s legal base from Delaware to Texas. Dell, who founded the company in Austin in 1984 shared a post of social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) in which he wrote, “Today, with 97% approval, Dell shareholders voted to bring our legal home to Texas. This is home and where we’ve always belonged. Texas gave us the talent, the universities, and the environment to build something that lasts. Proud to make it official. Let’s go.” This move from the Dell CEO comes days after Texas Governor Gregg Abbott welcomed the company with a “Welcome Home” message.In May this year, Michael Dell said that the company’s “Board of Directors has unanimously approved changing the jurisdiction of Dell Technologies’ state of incorporation from Delaware to its home state of Texas”. This “redomestication” of Dell is likely to be approved at the company’s annual stockholders meeting on June 25 and how the stake holders also voted in favour of the decision. Responding to this decision of Dell, exas Governor Greg Abbott shared an X post welcoming the laptop-maker. “Welcome home, @Dell,” Abbott wrote in the post. adding “For over 40 years, Texas has been where @MichaelDell built and innovated. Now, Dell Technologies is bringing its legal home to Texas.”
Article Summary: Michael Dell, the founder and CEO of Dell Technologies has pledged $750 million to the University of Texas at Austin. The gift will fund a new healthcare and research campus, including the nation’s first AI-native hospital. The new campus will feature a hospital designed around artificial intelligence, where AI systems will help doctors detect diseases earlier.

Article Title: After stressing electric grids, pushing utility bills and raising worries of water supply and pollution, data centers across America are running into a more basic problem: There are not enough…
Article Text:
A very human bottleneck for a very futuristic industry

How the AI hiring war is hurting homeowners

Why the data center labor shortage won't ease anytime soon

The AI data center boom was supposed to be America's new economic engine—a machine that fattens local tax coffers and mints jobs. But after straining power grids, driving up household utility bills and stoking fears over water and pollution, the industry has hit a wall that money alone can't knock down. There simply aren't enough skilled workers to build all the facilities being planned.The crunch is now serious enough that contractors are turning away business. "There is plenty more work we could take if we could possibly do it," Comfort Systems USA CFO William George told Bloomberg. He isn't alone. The combined project backlogs at Comfort Systems, Emcor Group and Sterling Infrastructure have jumped sixfold—far outpacing any growth in the pool of electricians and HVAC installers who actually do the work.For all of AI's sci-fi promise, its physical footprint runs on old-fashioned tradespeople. Data centers aren't ordinary construction jobs. They need high-voltage technicians, fiber-optic installers, controls engineers and commissioning teams—roles that take years of training to fill. That makes the labor pool almost impossible to expand as fast as investment has ballooned. Turner & Townsend found data centers are now the most constrained sector globally, with over 70% of the 112 markets it analyzed seeing tightening or overstretched contractor capacity.The roots run deep. Construction faces a graying workforce, too few young recruits and a thin pipeline of apprenticeships. Immigration crackdowns have squeezed things further, since foreign-born workers make up roughly a third of the construction trades.The pain is spilling into neighborhoods. In Abilene, Texas—home to the sprawling 4-million-square-foot Stargate facility backed by OpenAI and Oracle—homebuilder Gene Lantrip watched subcontractors lose crews to data centers offering far better pay. "It's hard to compete when contractors are paid $15 to $20 an hour, while the data centers offer $40 plus a per diem," he said. His houses now take two months longer to finish.In Arizona, remodeler Danny Niemela says pulling 200 electricians onto a single campus for a year guts the local workforce. An AC repair that once took two days can now stretch to five or six. Labor costs for licensed trades in the Valley region have climbed 12% to 18% over two years, he added.The numbers are stark. Recruiting firm iRecruit projects a shortfall of up to 499,000 workers for projects running 18 to 30 months. Associated Builders and Contractors says the industry needs 349,000 net new workers in 2026 just to meet demand, jumping to 456,000 in 2027.Some tech giants are trying to fix the pipeline themselves. Meta partnered with CBRE earlier this year on a workforce training initiative, hoping to widen the pool of qualified builders.But few expect a fast fix. Blue-collar stigma still runs deep, and training a skilled electrician takes years, not weeks. As Coastal Construction's Patrick Murphy put it, data centers didn't create the labor shortage—they exposed it. The industry has mastered attracting capital. Producing thousands of experienced tradespeople is proving to be the harder problem.
Article Summary: AI data center boom was supposed to be America's new economic engine. But the industry has hit a wall that money alone can't knock down. There simply aren't enough skilled workers to build all the facilities being planned. The crunch is now serious enough that contractors are turning away business.

Article Title: Chinese President Xi Jinping sends a strong message to American technology companies on AI; says: China is ready to…
Article Text:
Why open-source has become China’s biggest AI weapon

China’s new AI alliance and what it means for the US

Chinese President Xi Jinping used China’s biggest tech stage to draw a sharp line between how Beijing and Washington think about artificial intelligence—and the difference comes down to one word: openness. Speaking at the opening of the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on Friday, Xi urged countries to grab the “historic opportunity” of open-source AI and warned against letting a single nation dominate the technology.He never named the United States. He didn’t need to. With American labs like OpenAI and Anthropic guarding their frontier models behind closed doors, Xi’s pitch landed as a direct challenge to the way Silicon Valley operates. “China is ready to be more open, take more practical actions, and assume a more visionary perspective,” he said. His framing was blunt elsewhere too: AI development, he argued, “should not be a solo performance by a single country but a symphony of global collaboration. ”The message carries weight because Chinese open-weight models are no longer playing catch-up quietly. On the same day Xi spoke, Beijing-based Moonshot unveiled Kimi K3, which it called the world’s largest open AI model by parameter count.That arrival, alongside buzzy rivals like Z.ai’s GLM 5.2 and the earlier DeepSeek shock, shows how fast the gap with ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini is narrowing.American labs have taken the opposite route. Meta open-sourced its general Llama models but kept its proprietary Muse Spark private. OpenAI, despite the name, runs closed models. Anthropic does too—CEO Dario Amodei called open-source a “dangerous path” back in 2023, arguing companies lose the ability to moderate usage or revoke access once weights are public.Behind the speech sits real institutional muscle. A day earlier, Beijing launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation, or WAICO, a 29-nation coalition headquartered in Shanghai that includes Indonesia, Brazil, Russia, South Africa and Pakistan. Xi called it a “milestone in the history of world AI development,” pitching it as a home for Global South nations wanting a bigger say in how AI gets governed.That puts it in direct competition with Washington’s AI Opportunity Statement, which has drawn 35 countries. Only Kazakhstan appears on both lists—a sign that most nations haven’t hedged their bets yet.Xi also spent unusual time on AI safety, calling for systems to stay under human control and for early-warning and emergency-response mechanisms to guard against loss-of-control scenarios. He pledged 5,000 AI training and seminar slots for less advanced countries.That said, the openness has limits. Reuters reported this month that Beijing is weighing restrictions on overseas access to some of its top AI models, underscoring the tension between China’s open-source push and its national security agenda.
Article Summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping used China’s biggest tech stage to draw a sharp line between how Beijing and Washington think about artificial intelligence. Xi urged countries to grab the “historic opportunity” of open-source AI and warned against letting a single nation dominate the technology.

Article Title: USCIS sends alert for Fiscal Year 2027 H-1B visas, includes 'master's cap'; says: We have reached ...
Article Text:
USCIS says FY 2027 H-1B cap has been reached

“U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has received enough petitions to reach the congressionally mandated 65,000 H-1B visa regular cap and the 20,000 H-1B visa U.S. advanced degree exemption, known as the master’s cap, for fiscal year 2027,”

No second H-1B lottery expected

FY 2027 brought major changes to H-1B selection

The US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has announced that it has received enough petitions to meet the H-1B visa cap for Fiscal Year 2027, meaning there will be no additional lottery rounds. In an alert issued on July 17, 2026, the agency said it has reached both the 65,000 regular H-1B visa cap and the 20,000 U.S. advanced degree exemption, also known as the master's cap. The update marks the end of this year's H-1B cap selection process.In its alert, USCIS said it has received enough petitions to meet the congressionally mandated 65,000 regular H-1B visa cap as well as the 20,000 H-1B U.S. advanced degree exemption, commonly known as the master's cap, for Fiscal Year 2027.The agency will now continue processing petitions that were selected and filed under this year's cap.the alert read.The announcement means USCIS is not expected to conduct a second H-1B lottery for FY 2027.The agency typically holds another lottery only if it does not receive enough eligible petitions to meet the annual cap.This year, many applicants and employers had expected the possibility of another selection round because of several major changes to the H-1B process.Notably, fiscal Year 2027 was the first year USCIS used a wage-based lottery, replacing the previous random selection system. Under the new process, higher-paying jobs received better chances of selection. The number of H-1B registrations has reportedly declined sharply. About 211,600 registrations were submitted for FY 2027, down from 343,981 for FY 2026.The Trump administration also introduced a $100,000 H-1B petition fee in September 2025, prompting many employers to file fewer registrations and become more selective about the candidates they sponsored.
Article Summary: USCIS says it has received enough petitions to meet the H-1B visa cap for Fiscal Year 2027, meaning there will be no additional lottery rounds. The agency will now continue processing petitions that were selected and filed under this year's cap. This year was the first year USCIS used a wage-based lottery, replacing the previous random selection system.

Article Title: US judge to Meta's laid off employees: Cannot stop the company from job cuts, but can reconsider if you can provide how ...
Article Text:
Why US Judge declined an emergency request to stop Meta layoffs

Meta employees allege AI influenced layoff decisions

Facebook-parent Meta Platforms can reportedly go ahead with its planned layoffs of 26 employees who have sued the company, a US judge has ruled. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the decision comes after the Meta employees had asked the court to block the layoffs, alleging that the company selected them for job cuts using AI-powered evaluation tools that discriminated against workers with disabilities or those who had taken medical leave.However, while declining to halt the layoffs which are scheduled to begin next week, US District Judge William Orrick in Oakland, California, said the court “may reconsider” its decision if the employees provide additional evidence regarding “whether and how AI was used” in the company's workforce reduction.In a joint statement after the ruling, the employees' lawyers told Reuters, “The Court expressly stated that it may reconsider its determinations based on any additional evidence the parties provide regarding whether and how AI was used' in the reduction in force.”The Reuters report notes that the US District Judge Orrick rejected the employees' request for a temporary restraining order that would have prevented Meta from carrying out the layoffs while their claims proceed through private arbitration.In his written order, Orrick said the employees had not shown that losing their jobs would amount to the "irreparable harm" required for an emergency order blocking the layoffs.Meta declined to comment on the ruling. The company has also denied wrongdoing and has said that decisions related to the layoffs were made by humans.The lawsuit, filed earlier this week by 26 anonymous employees, claims Meta relied on AI-assisted systems to help determine which jobs would be eliminated during its latest workforce reduction.According to the complaint, the company used AI tools that measured productivity, AI token usage and AI adoption, which the employees allege disadvantaged workers who had taken medical leave or time off to care for family members.The plaintiffs also claim Meta used several internal AI-assisted systems to score and rank employees for layoffs, including a large language model assistant called “Metamate,” an employee-trained “second brain” that tracked communications and documents, and a productivity score generated from scanning keystrokes, screen content, emails and browser history.They allege these systems continued to collect performance-related data while employees were on legally protected leave, resulting in lower AI adoption scores that were later used in layoff selection.The employees remain on Meta's payroll but lost access to company systems in May and have not performed work since then, according to court filings. The layoffs are scheduled to be finalised on July 22 for many employees, with others expected to leave later in July or August.During a hearing this week, plaintiffs' lawyer Barbara Cowan argued that employees would lose more than salaries, saying, “There's no do-over for bonding with a new baby or giving birth or having active medical treatment.”Meta's lawyer Erin Connell responded that the workers were losing employer-subsidised health insurance rather than coverage altogether, and argued that such losses could be compensated later if the employees succeed in arbitration.The lawsuit is believed to be the first against a major US company alleging the use of AI tools in selecting employees for layoffs.
Article Summary: Meta Platforms can reportedly go ahead with its planned layoffs of 26 employees who have sued the company. US District Judge William Orrick in Oakland, California, said the court “may reconsider” its decision if the employees provide additional evidence regarding “whether and how AI was used” The lawsuit is believed to be the first against a major US company alleging the use of AI tools in selecting employees for layoffs.

Article Title: Employees at Jeff Bezos' SpaceX rival Blue Origin are upset over an unusual non-compete clause as they see it 'blocking' their way to become millionaires
Article Text:
New Blue Origin stock clause not for all ‘employees’

Florida: Approximately 4,000 employees.

Alabama: Approximately 1,600 employees.

Texas: Home to the company's primary launch site.

Following SpaceX's blockbuster IPO, several employees at Elon Musk's space company turned into millionaires overnight. This reportedly hit hard the staff working at rival Blue Origin, where they were said to have ‘broken morale’ as they’re sitting on effectively worthless stock options. To stem the frustration and stay competitive with SpaceX, Jeff Bezos ' space venture reportedly rolled out a new stock incentive plan for its employees. Now a new report claims that there’s a catch: the plan comes bundled with an unusual 18-month non-compete clause, and it may not be sitting well with everyone.According to a copy of the agreement seen by Business Insider, any employee who leaves Blue Origin and joins a direct competitor within 18 months will immediately forfeit 100% of their accumulated stock option – leaving many feeling trapped. Employment attorneys and corporate wealth managers noted that using non-competes to gatekeep equity is highly irregular for fast-growing private startups in the US.“If someone is planning to stay with the startup through an acquisition or IPO, this may not be important. But startups are staying private much longer than they did in earlier eras, so it's very likely that startup employees will leave before a companywide exit event,” Mary Russell, a startup equity attorney at Stock Option Counsel PC, told Business Insider.Because employees frequently jump between companies to advance their careers, the rule forces engineers to make a painful choice: stay out of the competitive job market for a year and a half, or walk away from their earned wealth. Former SpaceX employees who moved to Blue Origin noted that their prior contracts in the industry carried no such forfeiture penalties.Notably, the contract’s real-world implications do not affect all Blue Origin employees equally. As states like California and Washington enforce strict legal bans on non-compete agreements, workers located at Blue Origin's key West Coast facilities are exempt from the clause. However, the legal protection does not extend to the vast majority of the company’s 12,600-person workforce.A significant portion of the rocket manufacturer's labor pool is stationed in states with employer-friendly non-compete laws:Engineers and factory floor workers in these Southern hubs face far greater restrictions on cashing in their equity compared to their colleagues on the West Coast.
Article Summary: Blue Origin reportedly rolled out a new stock incentive plan for its employees. The plan comes bundled with an unusual 18-month non-compete clause, and it may not be sitting well with everyone. Any employee who leaves Blue Origin and joins a direct competitor within 18 months will immediately forfeit 100% of their accumulated stock option.

Article Title: What is ‘boss scam’ that market regulator SEBI has warned about: How fraudsters use WhatsApp, Microsoft Teams to target company employees
Article Text:
How the ‘ Boss Scam ’ works

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you feel comfortable verifying urgent money transfer requests through official channels? Yes, always No, not really 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

How to stay safe

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has issued a warning to corporate employees regarding a growing cyber fraud known as the “Boss Scam”. The market regulator stepped in after receiving alarming data from the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) showing a sharp rise in cases. The scam involves fraudsters impersonating Chief Executive Officers (CEOs), managing directors, and other senior corporate executives to trick unsuspecting staff members into transferring company funds.According to SEBI, cybercriminals are specifically targeting finance executives, accountants, and junior employees who have direct access to corporate bank accounts, news agency Reuters reported. The fraudsters launch their attacks using most commonly used communication channels, including corporate emails, WhatsApp, Microsoft Teams and other platforms.The scammer poses as a top-ranking company official and creates a false sense of urgency, instructing the employee to make an immediate financial transfer for a confidential or time-sensitive business deal. SEBI highlighted a dangerous technological variation of the scam that involves malicious software.First, scammers send compromised files or links to an employee. Once the employee opens the file, the hidden malware infects the device and hijacks active WhatsApp Web sessions or takes control of the system.Now with full access to a senior finance officer’s actual messaging account, the fraudster orders subordinate accounts employees finance-related requests. Understanding that the order has come from the ‘boss’, the employee adheres to it, essentially losing money in the end.“The fraudster gets access to the ⁠finance officer's WhatsApp account and then contacts accounts or finance employees, instructing them to make immediate payments to ⁠specified mule bank accounts,” SEBI said.To counter this wave of digital theft, the market regulator has ordered all SEBI-regulated entities, including brokerage firms, mutual fund houses and listed companies, to immediately update their internal safety protocols.For employees, it is advised that they should never transfer funds based entirely on text instructions received via social media, WhatsApp or chat apps. Secondly, any unusual or urgent request for money transfers must be verified through official, pre-established internal channels, such as a direct phone call or a face-to-face confirmation.Employees should refrain from opening unexpected attachments or links, especially those sent via messaging apps like WhatsApp Web, even if they appear to come from a known colleague or boss.
Article Summary: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has issued a warning to corporate employees regarding a growing cyber fraud known as the ‘Boss Scam’ The scam involves fraudsters impersonating Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) and other senior corporate executives to trick unsuspecting staff members into transferring company funds.

Article Title: Just a day after Chinese President Xi Jinping almost warned against US placing its own security above everyone else's, Anthropic announces changes to Claude Fable 5; says: Beginning July 20 ...
Article Text:
Anthropic overhauls Claude Fable 5 access plans



China President Xi takes aim at America’s ‘ Pax Silica ’



Anthropic announced a major adjustment for its highly sought-after frontier model, Claude Fable 5. The company said that starting July 20, it will overhaul how users can interact with the powerhouse AI. The announcement comes a day after Chinese President Xi Jinping delivered a critique of American technology blockades, and pushed forward China as an alternative to the booming technology.Amidst a backdrop of intense geopolitical maneuvering and capacity shortages, Anthropic announced an update addressing the heavy infrastructure strain and volatile demand surrounding its latest system.“Beginning July 20, Claude Fable 5 will be included in all Max and Team Premium plans, at 50% of limits,” the company said in a post on X (formerly Twitter). It added: “Pro and Team Standard users will continue to have access to Fable via usage credits, and will receive a one-time $100 credit. Demand for Fable has been challenging to predict, which is why we rolled it out to subscription plans in stages, extending access several times as we secured additional capacity. ”This means that Claude Fable 5 will now be natively included in all top-tier subscriptions but it will be capped at 50% of standard usage limits, and lower-tier subscribers will lose default access, migrating instead to a "usage credit" system.Anthropic also acknowledged user complaints over rolling capacity limits, “We know this has been frustrating, and we want to give you more certainty about what your plan includes. We are making access standard at 50% usage for the plans that use Fable most intensively.”The tech firm noted it is investing in additional processing chips and cloud capacity to stabilise limits in the near future.The sudden shift at Anthropic highlights the raw compute bottlenecks currently throttling Western tech giants. It comes precisely as Beijing positions its own massive, open-source technology ecosystem as a direct, unconstrained alternative for the world.Speaking at the opening ceremony of the premier World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) on Friday, July 17, Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined a dramatic counter-vision to the US-led technology alliance, commonly dubbed “Pax Silica.”Xi heavily targeted Washington's strict export restrictions and national security blockades, which recently forced US firms like Anthropic to pull proprietary commercial software models out of several overseas markets.“AI systems must remain under human control," Xi declared, pitching China as a collaborative global public good.
Article Summary: Anthropic overhauls Claude Fable 5 access plans starting July 20. Top-tier subscriptions will be capped at 50% of standard usage limits. Announcement comes a day after Chinese President Xi Jinping delivered a critique of American technology blockades.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai: AI is probably the most important thing humanity has ever worked on; I think of it as something more profound than electricity or fire
Article Text:
Google CEO Sundar Pichai



AI already powers everyday Google services

Google CEO Sundar Pichai once said that artificial intelligence (AI) will have a bigger impact on humanity than some of history's greatest inventions. Speaking at a town hall event in 2019, Sundar Pichai said AI is "probably the most important thing humanity has ever worked on" and described it as being "more profound than electricity or fire. " During the discussion, Pichai said AI has the potential to transform society in ways that go beyond earlier technological breakthroughs."AI is one of the most important things humanity is working on. It is more profound than, I dunno, electricity or fire," Pichai said.When interviewer Kara Swisher questioned the comparison, saying, "Fire? Fire is pretty good," Sundar Pichai stood by his view."Well, it kills people, too," he replied. "We have learned to harness fire for the benefits of humanity but we had to overcome its downsides too. So my point is, AI is really important, but we have to be concerned about it."Sundar Pichai then said people already use AI every day, often without realizing it. He then pointed to Google Translate, image search and Google Photos as examples of AI-powered tools used by billions of people.“AI is just making computers more intelligent and being able to do a wide variety of tasks," he said.The Google CEO also said AI could help address some of the world's biggest problems, including healthcare. “AI holds the potential for some of the biggest advances we are going to see," he said, adding that the technology could play a role in solving diseases such as cancer.At the same time, Sundar Pichai then stated that concerns about AI are valid. "It is right to be concerned, absolutely, you have to worry about it otherwise you are not going to solve it," he said.
Article Summary: Google CEO Sundar Pichai once said that artificial intelligence (AI) will have a bigger impact on humanity than some of history's greatest inventions. He said AI is "probably the most important thing humanity has ever worked on" The Google CEO also said AI could help address some of the world's biggest problems, including healthcare.

Article Title: San Francisco sends notice to Apple and Google: Remove these apps right away
Article Text:
Profiting from ‘illegal services’



Apple and Google respond to San Francisco notices

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg's Meta 'copies' Elon Musk's AI plan, makes an offer to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei asking...
Article Text:
Why Zuckerberg suddenly wants to rent out data centers

The chip shortage forcing AI rivals to share

Meta is in early talks to lease computing power to Anthropic in a deal that could be worth as much as $10 billion over two years, according to a New York Times report. If it closes, it would hand Mark Zuckerberg a brand-new line of business and pull Dario Amodei's AI lab deeper into a scramble for compute that shows no sign of easing.The move borrows straight from Elon Musk's playbook. Musk turned SpaceX's Colossus data centers into a rental business earlier this year, and Anthropic became its anchor tenant. Now Zuckerberg wants a slice of the same action, using the very data centers his investors keep grumbling about.Anthropic pitched the idea first, in JuneThe NYT reports that Anthropic proposed the deal in June, and Meta is weighing it. Anthropic would pay in monthly instalments across two years, with either side free to opt out early. The specifics are still moving around.The proposal is roughly a third the size of the SpaceX arrangement Anthropic signed in May. That one runs to $45 billion over three years, or $1.25 billion a month, for access to Musk's Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 clusters in Memphis. It too came with a 90-day exit clause, a nod to how quickly things shift in AI.There's an awkward wrinkle. Meta doesn't sell compute yet, so it has no machinery for a deal like this.One person familiar with the talks told the NYT that this has complicated the discussions.Meta plans to spend up to $145 billion this year, most of it on AI, more than double last year's $72 billion. Wall Street has been uneasy, questioning whether that spend is justified when Meta's own models trail those from Anthropic and OpenAI.Renting out spare capacity is Zuckerberg's answer. He has hinted at it for months. On a May investor call, he said companies approach Meta "almost every week" asking to buy compute at a premium, but that Meta had held off because it still had a use for the chips.The math is tempting. SpaceX has shown the model works, signing deals with Anthropic, Google and open-source startup Reflection. Meta has even hired Dave Brown, a former AWS executive, as it eyes the cloud business.Behind all this sits one stubborn problem: there aren't enough Nvidia chips to go around. Anthropic, now valued near $1 trillion and headed for an IPO, has seen demand explode since Claude Code took off. It places usage limits even on its top models like Fable.That scarcity is pushing rivals into bed together. Anthropic already leans on SpaceX and Amazon; adding Meta would spread its bets further. For Meta, an Anthropic contract offers revenue while its own AI products play catch-up.Both companies declined to comment. The talks are early and may lead nowhere. But the fact that two fierce competitors are even at the table says plenty about how precious compute has become — and how far Zuckerberg is willing to copy Musk to cash in on it.
Article Summary: Anthropic and Meta are in early talks to lease computing power to each other. The deal could be worth as much as $10 billion over two years. The move borrows straight from Elon Musk's playbook. Musk turned SpaceX's Colossus data centers into a rental business earlier this year.

Article Title: After Anthropic and OpenAI accuse Chinese AI companies of ‘distillation’, billionaire Chamath Palihapitiya says, ‘Cannot complain when you yourself have … ’
Article Text:
Anita Verma-Lallian and Chamath Palihapitiya

What US frontier AI labs claim



What Chamath Palihapitiya said

From Anthropic’s Fable model on the economic, moral, ethical and legal opinion of distillation of Anthropic’s Fable model:

Whether it’s a moral problem is genuinely contested. The labs trained their models on the open internet — copyrighted books, articles, code — largely without permission, and their fair-use defense is essentially “learning from data is transformative.” Distillation is the same argument turned against them: a model learning from another model’s outputs.

It’s hard to construct a moral principle that permits the first and forbids the second, which is why critics call the labs’ objections hypocritical rather than principled.

Distillation is contentious because it lets a smaller model absorb much of a frontier model’s capability by training on its outputs — effectively free-riding on billions of dollars of compute, data curation, and RLHF work.

The DeepSeek episode made this concrete: if you can extract 80% of the value of a $1B training run for $5M by querying the API, the economics of frontier labs get shaky.

That’s the core anxiety — it’s a moat problem before it’s anything else.

Legally, it’s mostly a contract issue, not a copyright one. Model outputs likely aren’t copyrightable (no human author), so the labs’ real weapon is terms of service — every major API prohibits using outputs to train competing models. But ToS violations are breach of contract, hard to detect, hard to prove, and nearly unenforceable against a foreign entity. There’s no statute against distillation itself. So the practical answer: it’s an economic problem dressed in legal clothing, with a moral argument that cuts both ways depending on whose training data you start counting from.

Tech billionaire and venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya has spoken on AI intellectual property debate following allegations from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic that accuse Chinese AI firms of “distillation” – the practice of copying the capabilities of a rival’s expensive AI model at a fraction of the cost. Pushing back against the complaints of the US frontier labs, Palihapitiya argues that tech giants cannot complain about competitors copying their systems when their own foundational AI models were built by scraping copyrighted human data from the open internet without permission.Palihapitiya’s comment came soon after the economic and moral defense of distillation was highlighted in an analysis of Anthropic's own Fable model. The company blamed Chinese AI companies to have used distillation to train their models, thereby, calling it ‘illegal’.Major AI labs have spent billions of dollars on computing power, data curation and human feedback to build their models. Yet, to gather their initial training datasets, they scraped millions of copyrighted books, news articles, and proprietary code from the public internet without compensating the original human creators.Their legal defense has rested on “fair use”.Palihapitiya points out in a long post on X (formerly Twitter) that distillation applies this exact same logic, only turned back onto the tech giants themselves. In distillation, a competitor's AI is simply “learning” from the output data of another AI. He also called the sudden anxiety gripping Silicon Valley driven by economics rather than ethics.Distillation ‘allowed’ Chinese companies to effectively free-ride on the astronomical research and development costs borne by US pioneers.
Article Summary: Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya has spoken on AI intellectual property debate. US labs OpenAI and Anthropic accuse Chinese AI firms of ‘distillation’ – the practice of copying the capabilities of a rival’s expensive AI model at a fraction of the cost. In distillation, a competitor's AI is simply “learning” from the output data of another AI.

Article Title: GIGABYTE launches GAMING A16, its first 'Made in India' gaming laptop
Article Text:
Gigabyte GAMING A16

GIGABYTE has launched its first Made in India gaming laptop, the GIGABYTE GAMING A16. It is powered by AMD Ryzen processor, and is aimed to deliver gaming as well as AI-ready computing experiences by utilising AMD technologies. To manufacture the lineup locally, GIGABYTE has partnered with Dixon Technologies. The collaboration combines GIGABYTE's global engineering and quality standards with Dixon's manufacturing capabilities.Sinclair Hsiao, vice president, global sales, GIGABYTE, visited India alongside senior leaders from the company's headquarters representing Product Management, Procurement, Materials Planning, and Quality Assurance.“The launch of our first Made in India gaming laptop lineup, powered by AMD Ryzen processors, is more than a manufacturing milestone, it represents GIGABYTE’s long-term commitment to the Indian market. India has become one of the most exciting technology and gaming markets in the world, and we believe Indian consumers deserve products built to the same uncompromising global standards that gamers everywhere expect from GIGABYTE.This is only the beginning. We will continue investing in India, strengthening our local manufacturing capabilities, and bringing more world-class gaming technologies closer to Indian consumers,” said Hsiao.The leadership team worked closely with Dixon Technologies to oversee every stage of the project, the outcome of a highly collaborative global effort, ensuring that the Made in India gaming laptop lineup meets GIGABYTE's rigorous global benchmarks for performance, reliability, and quality.The company says that India has emerged as one of the world's most dynamic PC and gaming markets, driven by a rapidly expanding community of gamers, creators, students, and technology enthusiasts. Recognising this momentum, GIGABYTE continues to deepen its investment in the country by expanding its local manufacturing capabilities while ensuring every product reflects the innovation, precision, and performance that define the GIGABYTE brand globally.Through local production backed by global expertise, the company is strengthening supply chain resilience, improving market responsiveness, and enabling Indian consumers to experience internationally acclaimed gaming technology manufactured within the country. This milestone marks the beginning of a new chapter in GIGABYTE's journey in India, one built on innovation, collaboration, and a shared vision for the future of gaming.

It is powered by AMD Ryzen processor, and is aimed to deliver gaming as well as AI-ready computing experiences by utilising AMD technologies. To manufacture the lineup locally, GIGabYTE has partnered with Dixon Technologies.
